## 10. Footguns

- **NEVER** mount `/var/run/docker.sock` or any kubelet CRI socket in any
  METIS pod. On Kubernetes, the only safe MCP runtime is
  `runtime: 'k8s-sse'` — already enforced in METIS code.
- `server.replicaCount` defaults to **2** (multi-replica). This is correct ONLY
  with the shared backends configured: a Postgres `DATABASE_URL` (#539, §0),
  `VECTOR_STORE=pgvector` (§9d — embedded LanceDB is NOT multi-replica safe; write
  divergence corrupts the index), `UPLOAD_STORAGE_BACKEND=s3` (§9f — otherwise
  uploads land on a per-pod RWO PVC other replicas can't read),
  `DISCUSSION_RATE_LIMIT_BACKEND=postgres` (§9b), `SSO_STATE_BACKEND=postgres`
  (§9c), and `SCHEDULER_LEADER_ELECTION=postgres` (§9e — otherwise the scheduler +
  background jobs fire on every replica). The chart's `metis.assertScalingBackends`
  helper enforces the hard requirements (Postgres `DATABASE_URL` + pgvector + S3)
  when `scaling.enforce=true` (set in `values-prod.yaml`); the chart default is
  `enforce=false` so a bare install renders, with `NOTES.txt` warning if N>1 lacks
  the backends. **If you have NOT set up the shared backends, pin
  `server.replicaCount=1`** (the `values-dev.yaml` profile does this).
- The chart does **not** install ESO, AWS LB Controller, EBS/EFS CSI, or
  cert-manager. Cluster prerequisites are owned by the operator.
- `gp3` StorageClass is **not** provisioned by EKS by default — you must
  apply the manifest in §3b.
- AWS VPC CNI alone does **not** enforce NetworkPolicy. Install Calico
  or switch to Cilium (the chart's `networkPolicy.cilium.enabled=true`
  toggle requires Cilium).

## Overview

When Requirements Analysis runs, METIS already resolves each requirement to the

### The #931 seeder must not be revived as-is

An LLM **seeder** — one that picks the code symbols BM25 will expand from — was
built (#931) and measured: table precision fell **0.42 → 0.29**. The mechanism is
recorded because it generalises: the seeder scored its own picks 1.0 and the
deterministic top-K 0.2, below `DEFAULT_MIN_CONFIDENCE` (0.3), so good BM25 seeds
were *dropped*. It shipped flag-off and is still flag-off.

The rule that came out of it: **prefer an LLM at the OUTPUT, or as a strictly
additive union, over an LLM at the SEED.** #936 (prune the output) and #1002
(union that preserves the base scores) both follow it. Any future seed-side lever
must leave the base candidates' original scores untouched — changing the max
silently re-normalises every deterministic confidence.

## Cost, and how it is metered (#1021)

An impact run makes **five** provider calls for a single changed requirement in
the default configuration: four per-requirement (#936 filter, #932 item narrative,
#1001 additive DDL, #1005 reconciler) plus one run-level overview, with at most
one repair retry each. Every one of them is individually switchable, which is the
point of the per-stage flags.

Until #1021 **none of those calls were metered**. They reached
`AIProvider.chat()` directly, and providers do not self-meter — every other
metered caller in the codebase records at the call site
(`discussions/ai-responder.ts`, `testcoverage/judge.ts`). The impact pipeline
never did, so `ai_token_usages` contained **zero** rows for the most
LLM-intensive feature in the product. That is not under-counting; it is absence.

The fix is a single chokepoint. `routes/impact-analysis.ts` builds one
`ImpactLlmRuntime` per run (`lib/impact-analysis/impact-llm-runtime.ts`) and
every stage's provider goes through `runtime.instrument(provider, stage)`. The
decorator records one `AITokenUsage` row per completed call:

| Column | Value |
|---|---|
| `agentStep` | `impact.<stage>` — `impact.table-filter`, `impact.additive-ddl`, `impact.clause-reconcile`, `impact.summary-item`, `impact.summary-run`, `impact.entity-seeds`, `impact.seeding` |
| `projectId` | the project the engine was working on when the call was made |
| `sessionId` | one lazily-created `AISession` per run (no LLM call ⇒ no session row) |
| `userId` | the actor who started the run |
| `estimatedCostUsd` | the usual `estimateUsageCostUsd` cache-aware estimate |

Query the whole feature with `agentStep LIKE 'impact.%'`, or one stage exactly.

### Premium requests

GitHub Copilot meters paid usage in **premium requests**. The rules that matter:

- **One user prompt in agent/chat mode = 1 premium request, multiplied by the
  model's multiplier.** A cheaper model has a smaller multiplier; a frontier model
  has a larger one. (See the authoritative, frequently-updated list:
  [GitHub Copilot — auto model selection & multipliers](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/models/auto-model-selection).)
- **Copilot code review costs 13 premium requests per review** (as of 2026-06-01).
  This is why the Orchestrator caps review cycles and only re-reviews after fixes are
  actually pushed — every wasted review cycle is expensive.
- Tool calls the model makes while servicing your prompt do **not** each cost a new
  premium request, but they **do** consume context-window tokens, which is the *other*
  cost you are managing (see below).

> **Two distinct budgets.** (a) *Premium requests* — billed, per-prompt, model-weighted.
> Fewer, better prompts and cheaper models reduce this. (b) *Context-window tokens* —
> the working memory of a single request. Bloated context degrades answer quality and
> can force truncation/compaction. Most techniques in this doc reduce **both**.

### How a BA sees it, and why it is not persisted on its own

Gaps are fed to the #932 summarizer as **facts**, and the per-item prompt gains a
"POSSIBLE COVERAGE GAPS" block plus one instruction to close with an
incompleteness warning. Only the **table name** enters the grounding allowlist —
the model-written `clause`/`rationale` carry no grounding authority, exactly as the
untrusted requirement text does not.

Two alternatives were rejected for the prototype:

- **A dedicated persisted column/table.** Needs a Prisma dual-schema migration
  plus a Postgres baseline edit. Correct once the signal has earned it; premature
  before the measurement below.
- **Appending the advisory to the persisted `summary` string after generation.**
  That column's documented invariant is "grounded ⊆ engine facts"; a gap table is
  by definition *not* an affected-table fact, so appending post-hoc would quietly
  violate the contract the column advertises.

With gaps empty — which is what a disabled reconciler, an unavailable provider or
a clean requirement all produce — the summarizer prompt is byte-identical to
pre-#1005, so no existing narrative shifts.

### Rules of thumb

- **Default to Auto** for general work; it routes each task to the cheapest capable model.
- **Pin a cheap model on read-only agents** (exploration, summarization) — but see the
  next rule before assuming "read-only" means "cheap".
- **Match the model to the blast radius, not to the invocation count.** Dispatch frequency
  measures how often an agent runs, not how hard its task is, so it cannot justify a
  downgrade on its own. Tier *up* where a cheap mistake is copied downstream: the
  lowest-volume agent whose output every later agent is graded against is the cheapest
  place in the fleet to buy accuracy. That is why METIS moved `research` from `haiku` to
  `sonnet` in #1146 — one wrong claim in a research summary is copied into an epic and
  then into every sub-issue.
- **Do not downgrade the quality gates.** Code review and security reasoning are where
  errors are most expensive — keep those on a strong model (`inherit`/frontier). Saving
  a few tokens on the gate that prevents bad merges is a false economy.
- **Escalate, don't start high.** Try a mid model; only move to frontier if it stalls.
- **One hard prompt beats five vague ones.** A precise prompt to a strong model often
  costs less in total than many cheap-but-thrashing round-trips.

### Why the session itself is a cost

Everything already in the current window — files read, tool results, prior reasoning,
completed todos — **is re-sent with every new prompt you type in that session.** The
conversation is cumulative: a turn 30 prompts deep carries the weight of all 29 before
it. That has three consequences:

1. **You keep paying** (in context-window tokens) for old work on every subsequent turn.
2. When the window fills, the assistant triggers **compaction** — it summarizes/drops
   older content. The summary is lossy and can mangle details you still cared about.
3. **Stale context degrades quality.** The model anchors on earlier files and decisions
   that are no longer relevant, producing worse answers for the new task.

## 10. Avoiding "vibe coding"

**Vibe coding** is accepting AI output because it *looks* right — no spec, no tests, no
verification. It feels fast and produces unmaintainable, insecure, or subtly broken code.
"Let the AI do as much as possible" and "don't vibe code" are **not** in tension: the
resolution is to make autonomy **bounded by verification, not by trust.**

The model is allowed to do a lot *because* its output must pass gates it cannot talk its
way around:

| Guardrail | Where it lives | What it prevents |
|-----------|----------------|------------------|
| **Specs first** | `epic-planner` / `code-planner` write acceptance criteria before code | Building the wrong thing |
| **TDD + ≥80% coverage** | `code-issue` skill | Untested code paths, regressions |
| **OWASP Top 10 review** | `code-review` skill | Injection, broken auth, secrets, SSRF, etc. |
| **`disallowedTools: Write, Edit` on the reviewer** | `code-review` agent | The reviewer "fixing" instead of reporting; rubber-stamping |
| **CI must be green** | review gate + Orchestrator | Merging broken builds (even pre-existing failures) |
| **Dependency CVE audit** | Orchestrator SECURITY AUDIT phase | Pulling in vulnerable packages |
| **Capped review cycles (max 2)** | Orchestrator | Endless expensive review loops |
| **CHANGELOG discipline** | review + contribution rules | Undocumented user-facing changes |
| **Memory / learnings files** | `/memories/`, repo memory | Re-deriving the same facts every session (also saves tokens) |

### Practices that keep you out of the vibe-coding trap

1. **Write the acceptance criteria before the code.** If you can't state how you'll know
   it works, the model can't either.
2. **Demand tests with the change**, and read them — a test that passes when the
   implementation is wrong is worse than no test.
3. **Read the diff, not the vibe.** Skim every changed file; don't approve on summary
   alone.
4. **Keep the human in the loop at decision points** (repo creation, schema changes,
   force-push, deletes) — these are deliberately not automated.
5. **Make the model cite evidence** (file:line, docs) rather than assert. This is also a
   token *saver* because it discourages the model from re-reading everything to bluff.
6. **Prefer small, verifiable increments** over one giant generated change you can't
   review.

> Autonomy and rigor compound: precise specs and hard gates let you safely hand the model
> *more* work, while also reducing the exploratory token-thrash that comes from vague
> instructions.

### What an agent costs

When an agent runs, its **system prompt (the whole `.agent.md` body)** and frontmatter
enter context. In Copilot, the Orchestrator pattern runs Plan → Implement → Review in
one session by calling specialized agents as **subagents**.

isolated context window.** It does *not* inherit the caller's conversation history. It

# Impact Analysis — which stages are LLM-backed, which are deterministic, and why

**Status:** current as of issue #1025 (epic #999), 2026-07-22.
**Audience:** anyone about to add, remove, or re-tune an LLM call in Impact Analysis.

> **#1025 — four of these stages now default ON.** An impact analysis on an
> install with an AI provider configured makes **five provider calls and costs
> roughly $0.05 and ~18 s per changed requirement**, where before it cost nothing
> and ran in well under a second. Read
> [Defaults, and what they cost](#defaults-and-what-they-cost-1025) before
> deploying, and disable any stage you do not want with its `=0` kill-switch.

This document exists so the question *"is this stage LLM-backed?"* never has to be
re-derived by grepping every provider call site again. It also records the
**reasons** for each side of the split, because the reasons are what stop a
well-meaning change from re-opening a measured regression.
relevant:
### Premium requests

GitHub Copilot meters paid usage in **premium requests**. The rules that matter:

- **One user prompt in agent/chat mode = 1 premium request, multiplied by the
  model's multiplier.** A cheaper model has a smaller multiplier; a frontier model
  has a larger one. (See the authoritative, frequently-updated list:
  [GitHub Copilot — auto model selection & multipliers](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/models/auto-model-selection).)
- **Copilot code review costs 13 premium requests per review** (as of 2026-06-01).
  This is why the Orchestrator caps review cycles and only re-reviews after fixes are
  actually pushed — every wasted review cycle is expensive.
- Tool calls the model makes while servicing your prompt do **not** each cost a new
  premium request, but they **do** consume context-window tokens, which is the *other*
  cost you are managing (see below).

> **Two distinct budgets.** (a) *Premium requests* — billed, per-prompt, model-weighted.
> Fewer, better prompts and cheaper models reduce this. (b) *Context-window tokens* —
> the working memory of a single request. Bloated context degrades answer quality and
> can force truncation/compaction. Most techniques in this doc reduce **both**.

### Why subagents *save* tokens

A subagent's verbose work — test output, dependency audits, doc fetches, file dumps —
stays inside its isolated window. Only the **summary** returns to the caller. Routing
high-volume tasks to subagents is the single most effective way to keep the main
conversation lean.

```text
Main thread asks:  "Run the full test suite and tell me what failed."
  └─ subagent: runs vitest (8,000 tokens of output) in its own window
     └─ returns to main thread: "3 tests failed in auth.test.ts: <names + reasons>"  (120 tokens)
```

## 11. Worked example

A realistic "add a feature" run, annotated with where tokens go and how each lever helps.

```text
USER: "Add rate limiting to the /api/m365/cleanup endpoint, with tests and a PR."

1. ORCHESTRATOR (balanced model) — delegates; keeps main thread tiny.

2. → research subagent (haiku, mcpServers: context7)
     - looks up express-rate-limit usage via context7 (docs, not source)
     - returns a 150-token summary          ← verbose doc text stayed in the subagent

3. → code-planner subagent (balanced)
     - graphify query "m365 cleanup route"  ← ~2k tokens instead of reading the router tree
     - writes acceptance criteria + 1 sub-issue   ← spec-first, not vibe

4. → code-issue subagent (balanced/inherit)
     - reads ONLY the flagged route file (targeted range, not the whole module)
     - TDD: writes a failing test, implements, runs `vitest run` in the subagent
       (8k tokens of test output stay in the subagent)   ← returns "all green" to main
     - ≥80% coverage enforced               ← gate, not vibe
     - opens PR, updates CHANGELOG [Unreleased]

5. ORCHESTRATOR — SECURITY AUDIT phase
     - `pnpm audit` + OSV.dev lookups for any new dep   ← blocks High/Critical

6. → code-review subagent (strong/inherit, disallowedTools: Write,Edit)
     - OWASP pass (A04 rate limiting is literally the change), CI must be green
     - graphify path <route> <callers> to catch un-updated callers
     - publishes structured review; verdict APPROVE
     - review = 13 premium requests, so it runs ONCE, after fixes are in

7. ORCHESTRATOR — reports: epic/issue #, PR #, coverage, audit result, verdict.
```

Token hot-spots avoided: the express-rate-limit docs, the test output, and the router
exploration were the three largest token sinks — and all three were absorbed by
subagents or replaced by a graphify query, never touching the main window.

## 2. Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|-----------|
| **Token** | The unit models read/write. ~4 characters / ~0.75 words of English. Pricing and context limits are denominated in tokens. |
| **Context window** | The maximum tokens a model can consider for a single request. Shared across system prompt, instructions, tool schemas, files read, and tool outputs. |
| **Premium request** | Copilot's paid billing unit. 1 per agent/chat prompt × the model's multiplier. Code review = 13. |
| **Model multiplier** | A per-model factor applied to the premium-request cost. Small/fast models are cheaper; frontier models cost more. |
| **Agent** (`.github/agents/*.agent.md` for Copilot | A persona defined by a system prompt + YAML frontmatter (allowed tools, model, sub-agents, handoffs). Frontmatter is loaded when the agent runs. |
| **Subagent** | An agent invoked by another agent (`runSubagent`). Runs in an **isolated context window**; only its final summary returns to the caller. The key tool for keeping verbose work out of the main conversation. |
| **Skill** (`.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) | A reusable, step-by-step workflow. Only its **name + description** sit in context until it is invoked; then the **full body loads** and persists for the rest of the session. |
| **Instruction file** (`.github/instructions/*.instructions.md`) | File-pattern-scoped coding rules. Pulled into context when you touch a matching file (via `applyTo` globs). |
| **Always-on context** (`copilot-instructions.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`) | Project rules auto-loaded into (nearly) every request/subagent. The most expensive lines in the repo because they are paid repeatedly. |
| **MCP server** | A Model Context Protocol server exposing tools (e.g. `github`, `context7`, `tavily`, `playwright`). Defined in `.vscode/mcp.json` / `.mcp.json`. |
| **Tool schema** | The name + description + parameter spec of a tool. Every *enabled* tool's schema occupies context so the model knows the tool exists. |

## 12. Quick-reference checklist

**Before exploring the codebase**
- [ ] `graphify-out/` present? → `graphify query/path/explain` before any wide grep.
- [ ] Need line-level source only graphify doesn't store? → read **targeted ranges**.

**When configuring agents/skills**
- [ ] Always-on files (`CLAUDE.md`, `copilot-instructions.md`) lean? (paid every subagent)
- [ ] Agent `tools:` restricted to what it needs? Reviewer has `disallowedTools: Write,Edit`?
- [ ] MCP servers scoped per agent (`mcpServers:`)?
- [ ] Skill `description` leads with `USE WHEN` / `NOT FOR`?
- [ ] `SKILL.md` focused on the common path; rare reference pushed to supporting files?
- [ ] Duplicated rules (shell hygiene, etc.) deduped to one source?

**When running work**
- [ ] High-volume output (tests, audits, doc fetches, exploration) routed to a subagent?
- [ ] Model matched to difficulty? (cheap for research, strong for the review gate)
- [ ] `model: Auto` for mixed work; escalate only when a mid model stalls?
- [ ] Review run **once**, after fixes are pushed (13 premium requests each)?
- [ ] Finish the task, then start a fresh session instead of one ballooning thread?

**To stay out of vibe coding**
- [ ] Acceptance criteria written before code?
- [ ] Tests included, read, and meaningful?
- [ ] Diff reviewed file-by-file, not approved on summary?
- [ ] Security (OWASP) + CVE audit + green CI enforced as hard gates?
- [ ] Humans confirm irreversible actions (repo create, schema change, force-push)?

### Practical agent rules

- **Restrict `tools:`** to what the agent actually needs. Unused tool schemas are dead
  weight in that agent's window. Example: the review agent does not need write tools.
- **Set `model:` per agent** to the cheapest model that can do the job (see §8).
- **Scope MCP servers to the agent** (`mcpServers:` in Claude Code) so a research agent
  doesn't carry the Playwright browser tool schemas, and a reviewer doesn't carry write
  tools.
- **Use Explore/Plan (Claude Code) or a dedicated research subagent (Copilot)** for
  "where is X / what calls Y" questions — they are the cheapest way to search.
- **Keep the agent body tight.** It is the system prompt; every word is paid each run.

#### A `tools:` entry is a declaration, not a guarantee

Note what is *absent* from that example: `Glob` and `Grep`. All seven agents declared both
and none could call either. `tools: Read, Bash, Glob, Grep` resolves to exactly
`["Read","Bash"]`, and a default session with no agent and no restrictions offers neither, so
this build does not **expose** those names — it ships `ToolSearch` instead (CLI 2.1.220,
measured; no settings file removes them). That is non-exposure, not absence: `strings` on the
binary does show a `Glob` definition behind a conditional, and whether exposure is gated on
configuration was not determined. It does not matter to the rule — in every shape measured,
declaring them is dead text. A live `code-review` dispatch calling them got
*"No such tool available: Glob. Glob is not available in this session — find files with
`find` via the Bash tool instead."*

That is the **third** instance of one class, after #1162 (`Skill` omitted from an allowlist)
and #1163 (`memory:` with no writable store): frontmatter promising a capability the harness
never delivers, failing only at call time, deep inside a dispatch, where nobody reads it.
`pnpm agents:verify` now rejects any `tools:` entry in `UNAVAILABLE_TOOLS`, and separately
rejects a `tools:` key that is **present but empty** — measured, that resolves to a tool list
of length **0**, not to inherit-everything, so it silently produces an agent that can do
nothing (#1168). Agents search with `grep`/`find` via `Bash`, or dispatch `Explore`.

### How an inbound message is ingested

1. **Activity type.** Only `message` activities carry content; everything else is
   ignored.
2. **Bot-own-message guard.** A proactive message #550 sent comes back as an
   activity whose `from.id === recipient.id` (the bot's own id) — ignored before
   any work (see [Loop guard round trip](#loop-guard-round-trip)).
3. **Resolve the link.** `getByConversation(workspaceId, conversationId)` (#549).
   No active link → the channel is not bridged → ignored.
4. **Text.** The leading bot `@mention` markup is stripped (other users'
   mentions preserved); an empty / mention-only message is skipped.
5. **Resolve the sender.** `resolveUserFromAadObjectId(tenantId, aadObjectId)`
   (#549), with `tenantId` taken from the activity's `channelData.tenant.id`,
   then `conversation.tenantId`, then the link's recorded tenant.
6. **Unmapped sender → never attributed to nobody.** When the resolver returns
   `null`, ingestion is **skipped** and a one-time, per-conversation, best-effort
   hint is posted back to the channel inviting the user to link their METIS
   account. No message is created.
7. **Member/tenant authorization.** Identity is not authorization — the resolved
   user is run through `canAccessThread` at the **lowest privilege**
   (`role: "reader"`, so access must be earned through real project membership,
   never a fabricated admin role). A resolved-but-unauthorized sender is rejected
   (forbidden); a link pointing at a missing/soft-deleted thread reports
   not-found.
8. **Create.** `createHumanDiscussionMessage({ ..., origin: "teams" })` — the
   `origin: "teams"` is what makes the #550 outbound mirror skip it.

## 3. The mental model

Picture the context window as a fixed-size desk. Five things compete for desk space on
every request:

```
┌───────────────────────── context window ─────────────────────────┐
│ system prompt + agent persona                                     │
│ ALWAYS-ON instruction files (copilot-instructions.md / CLAUDE.md) │ ← paid every time
│ tool schemas for every ENABLED tool                               │ ← paid every time
│ invoked skill bodies (persist once loaded)                        │
│ files you read + every tool result + conversation history         │ ← grows during work
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The optimization strategy follows directly:

| If this is large… | …do this |
|---|---|
| Always-on instruction files | Keep them lean; they are paid on every request **and every subagent spawn**. |
| Tool schemas | Enable only the servers/tools you need; rely on tool search to defer the rest. |
| Skill bodies | Keep `SKILL.md` focused; push rarely-needed detail to supporting files read on demand. |
| Files read + tool results | Use graphify to answer structural questions; read targeted line ranges, not whole files; route high-volume output to subagents. |
| Conversation history | Finish a task, then start a fresh session rather than letting one balloon. |

#### `memory:` needs a write tool, and a committed index

There is **no `memory:` line in that example**, and that is the point. `memory: project`
gives an agent a store under `.claude/agent-memory/<name>/`, and it earns its keep — one
`code-issue` memory recording that a named export in `synthesis.ts` breaks ~48 tests was
handed to three later agents and none of them hit it. But the declaration is only half of
the capability, and #1146 granted it to `code-review` and `ui-vision` *alongside*
`disallowedTools: Write, Edit`. Measured first-hand on a live `code-review` dispatch
(#1163) — `ui-vision` was not probed separately, it had the identical pairing:

- Claude Code injects the **entire** memory protocol into the system prompt regardless —
  roughly a third of the agent's instructions, telling it to use the `Write` tool.
- **The harness creates the store directory** at dispatch (it appeared empty and freshly
  timestamped mid-probe) **but no `MEMORY.md`**.
- The agent's own `Write` then fails: *"No such tool available: Write. Write exists but is
  not enabled in this context."* So the docs' "Read, Write, and Edit tools are
  automatically enabled so the subagent can manage its memory files" does **not** override
  an explicit **`disallowedTools:`** denial. (#1163 stated this more broadly, as "does not
  override the agent's own `tools:` / `disallowedTools:`". The `tools:` half of that is
  **wrong** — see the 2x2 below, where the injection does beat a `tools:` allowlist that
  merely omits the write tools. #1163 could not tell the two apart because its probe subject
  held both at once.)

Nothing errors unless the agent happens to attempt a write, so the only symptom is a store
that stays empty forever. `pnpm agents:verify` therefore fails on a declared `memory:`
scope that has no reachable store — `disallowedTools` denying **both** `Write` and `Edit`,
or (for `project` scope, which is shared *through version control*) a `MEMORY.md` index that
is not **tracked in git**.

### Progressive disclosure: the whole point of skills

A skill is a workflow document. Copilot/Claude use **progressive disclosure**:

1. **Always in context:** only the skill's **name + `description`** (a few dozen
   tokens). This is how the model knows the skill exists and when to use it.
2. **On invocation:** the **full `SKILL.md` body** loads — and then **stays in context**
   for the rest of the session.

So a 560-line skill costs ~30 tokens until used, then ~8k tokens for the rest of the
session once triggered. Two consequences:

- **Write descriptions that trigger correctly the first time.** A vague description
  causes the wrong skill to fire (wasting a load) or the right one to be missed. Lead
  with the trigger phrase and the "use when / not for" boundaries.
- **Keep `SKILL.md` focused on the common path.** Push rarely-needed reference (large
  lookup tables, exhaustive examples, error-recovery matrices) into supporting files
  that the agent reads *only when it actually needs them*.

> **When to split a skill.** Split only when a large fraction of the body is **rarely
> needed**. If the bulk is the substance the workflow uses on every run (e.g. the OWASP
> table in `code-review`), splitting just adds a read round-trip when the detail is
> needed and saves little — don't fragment a tuned workflow for its own sake. We **did**
> remove duplicated shell-hygiene rules from `code-review/SKILL.md` because that text is
> already in `CLAUDE.md` / `copilot-instructions.md` — dedup is a free win; splitting
> load-bearing content is not.

### Rules of thumb

- **Default to Auto** for general work; it routes each task to the cheapest capable model.
- **Pin a cheap model on read-only agents** (exploration, summarization) — but see the
  next rule before assuming "read-only" means "cheap".
- **Match the model to the blast radius, not to the invocation count.** Dispatch frequency
  measures how often an agent runs, not how hard its task is, so it cannot justify a
  downgrade on its own. Tier *up* where a cheap mistake is copied downstream: the
  lowest-volume agent whose output every later agent is graded against is the cheapest
  place in the fleet to buy accuracy. That is why METIS moved `research` from `haiku` to
  `sonnet` in #1146 — one wrong claim in a research summary is copied into an epic and
  then into every sub-issue.
- **Do not downgrade the quality gates.** Code review and security reasoning are where
  errors are most expensive — keep those on a strong model (`inherit`/frontier). Saving
  a few tokens on the gate that prevents bad merges is a false economy.
- **Escalate, don't start high.** Try a mid model; only move to frontier if it stalls.
- **One hard prompt beats five vague ones.** A precise prompt to a strong model often
  costs less in total than many cheap-but-thrashing round-trips.

## Cost, and how it is metered (#1021)

An impact run makes **five** provider calls for a single changed requirement in
the default configuration: four per-requirement (#936 filter, #932 item narrative,
#1001 additive DDL, #1005 reconciler) plus one run-level overview, with at most
one repair retry each. Every one of them is individually switchable, which is the
point of the per-stage flags.

Until #1021 **none of those calls were metered**. They reached
`AIProvider.chat()` directly, and providers do not self-meter — every other
metered caller in the codebase records at the call site
(`discussions/ai-responder.ts`, `testcoverage/judge.ts`). The impact pipeline
never did, so `ai_token_usages` contained **zero** rows for the most
LLM-intensive feature in the product. That is not under-counting; it is absence.

The fix is a single chokepoint. `routes/impact-analysis.ts` builds one
`ImpactLlmRuntime` per run (`lib/impact-analysis/impact-llm-runtime.ts`) and
every stage's provider goes through `runtime.instrument(provider, stage)`. The
decorator records one `AITokenUsage` row per completed call:

### Why the session itself is a cost

Everything already in the current window — files read, tool results, prior reasoning,
completed todos — **is re-sent with every new prompt you type in that session.** The
conversation is cumulative: a turn 30 prompts deep carries the weight of all 29 before
it. That has three consequences:

1. **You keep paying** (in context-window tokens) for old work on every subsequent turn.
2. When the window fills, the assistant triggers **compaction** — it summarizes/drops
   older content. The summary is lossy and can mangle details you still cared about.
3. **Stale context degrades quality.** The model anchors on earlier files and decisions
   that are no longer relevant, producing worse answers for the new task.

### Progressive disclosure: the whole point of skills

A skill is a workflow document. Copilot/Claude use **progressive disclosure**:

1. **Always in context:** only the skill's **name + `description`** (a few dozen

  causes the wrong skill to fire (wasting a load) or the right one to be missed. Lead
  with the trigger phrase and the "use when / not for" boundaries.
- **Keep `SKILL.md` focused on the common path.** Push rarely-needed reference (large
  lookup tables, exhaustive examples, error-recovery matrices) into supporting files
  that the agent reads *only when it actually needs them*.

> needed**. If the bulk is the substance the workflow uses on every run (e.g. the OWASP
> table in `code-review`), splitting just adds a read round-trip when the detail is
> needed and saves little — don't fragment a tuned workflow for its own sake. We **did**

The Claude Code fleet as it stands (`.claude/agents/`, audited in #1146 — `pnpm
agents:verify` keeps the definitions honest):

| Agent | Model on disk | Why |

| `code-planner` | `inherit` | Whole-system epics need reasoning depth |
| `code-issue` | `inherit` | Long-horizon agentic work across many files |
| `code-review` | `inherit` | It's the quality gate — do not cut corners here |
| `adversarial-reviewer` | `inherit` | Told to disprove a change; weak reasoning finds nothing |
| `e2e-test` | `sonnet` | Mechanical once acceptance criteria are mapped |
| `ui-vision` | `inherit` | Browser-driven, but must judge what it sees |

There is deliberately no `orchestrator` — the main session orchestrates and dispatches

### Rules of thumb

- **Default to Auto** for general work; it routes each task to the cheapest capable model.
- **Pin a cheap model on read-only agents** (exploration, summarization) — but see the
  next rule before assuming "read-only" means "cheap".
- **Match the model to the blast radius, not to the invocation count.** Dispatch frequency
  measures how often an agent runs, not how hard its task is, so it cannot justify a
  downgrade on its own. Tier *up* where a cheap mistake is copied downstream: the
  lowest-volume agent whose output every later agent is graded against is the cheapest
  place in the fleet to buy accuracy. That is why METIS moved `research` from `haiku` to
  `sonnet` in #1146 — one wrong claim in a research summary is copied into an epic and
  then into every sub-issue.
- **Do not downgrade the quality gates.** Code review and security reasoning are where
  errors are most expensive — keep those on a strong model (`inherit`/frontier). Saving
  a few tokens on the gate that prevents bad merges is a false economy.
- **Escalate, don't start high.** Try a mid model; only move to frontier if it stalls.
- **One hard prompt beats five vague ones.** A precise prompt to a strong model often
  costs less in total than many cheap-but-thrashing round-trips.

#### A `tools:` entry is a declaration, not a guarantee

Note what is *absent* from that example: `Glob` and `Grep`. All seven agents declared both
and none could call either. `tools: Read, Bash, Glob, Grep` resolves to exactly
`["Read","Bash"]`, and a default session with no agent and no restrictions offers neither, so
this build does not **expose** those names — it ships `ToolSearch` instead (CLI 2.1.220,
measured; no settings file removes them). That is non-exposure, not absence: `strings` on the
binary does show a `Glob` definition behind a conditional, and whether exposure is gated on
configuration was not determined. It does not matter to the rule — in every shape measured,
declaring them is dead text. A live `code-review` dispatch calling them got
*"No such tool available: Glob. Glob is not available in this session — find files with
`find` via the Bash tool instead."*

That is the **third** instance of one class, after #1162 (`Skill` omitted from an allowlist)
and #1163 (`memory:` with no writable store): frontmatter promising a capability the harness
never delivers, failing only at call time, deep inside a dispatch, where nobody reads it.
`pnpm agents:verify` now rejects any `tools:` entry in `UNAVAILABLE_TOOLS`, and separately
rejects a `tools:` key that is **present but empty** — measured, that resolves to a tool list
of length **0**, not to inherit-everything, so it silently produces an agent that can do
nothing (#1168). Agents search with `grep`/`find` via `Bash`, or dispatch `Explore`.

#### `memory:` needs a write tool, and a committed index

There is **no `memory:` line in that example**, and that is the point. `memory: project`
gives an agent a store under `.claude/agent-memory/<name>/`, and it earns its keep — one
`code-issue` memory recording that a named export in `synthesis.ts` breaks ~48 tests was
handed to three later agents and none of them hit it. But the declaration is only half of
the capability, and #1146 granted it to `code-review` and `ui-vision` *alongside*
`disallowedTools: Write, Edit`. Measured first-hand on a live `code-review` dispatch
(#1163) — `ui-vision` was not probed separately, it had the identical pairing:

- Claude Code injects the **entire** memory protocol into the system prompt regardless —
  roughly a third of the agent's instructions, telling it to use the `Write` tool.
- **The harness creates the store directory** at dispatch (it appeared empty and freshly
  timestamped mid-probe) **but no `MEMORY.md`**.
- The agent's own `Write` then fails: *"No such tool available: Write. Write exists but is
  not enabled in this context."* So the docs' "Read, Write, and Edit tools are
  automatically enabled so the subagent can manage its memory files" does **not** override
  an explicit **`disallowedTools:`** denial. (#1163 stated this more broadly, as "does not
  override the agent's own `tools:` / `disallowedTools:`". The `tools:` half of that is
  **wrong** — see the 2x2 below, where the injection does beat a `tools:` allowlist that
  merely omits the write tools. #1163 could not tell the two apart because its probe subject
  held both at once.)

Nothing errors unless the agent happens to attempt a write, so the only symptom is a store
that stays empty forever. `pnpm agents:verify` therefore fails on a declared `memory:`
scope that has no reachable store — `disallowedTools` denying **both** `Write` and `Edit`,
or (for `project` scope, which is shared *through version control*) a `MEMORY.md` index that
is not **tracked in git**.

## 12. Quick-reference checklist

**Before exploring the codebase**
- [ ] `graphify-out/` present? → `graphify query/path/explain` before any wide grep.
- [ ] Need line-level source only graphify doesn't store? → read **targeted ranges**.

**When configuring agents/skills**
- [ ] Always-on files (`CLAUDE.md`, `copilot-instructions.md`) lean? (paid every subagent)
- [ ] Agent `tools:` restricted to what it needs? Reviewer has `disallowedTools: Write,Edit`?
- [ ] MCP servers scoped per agent (`mcpServers:`)?
- [ ] Skill `description` leads with `USE WHEN` / `NOT FOR`?
- [ ] `SKILL.md` focused on the common path; rare reference pushed to supporting files?
- [ ] Duplicated rules (shell hygiene, etc.) deduped to one source?

**When running work**
- [ ] High-volume output (tests, audits, doc fetches, exploration) routed to a subagent?
- [ ] Model matched to difficulty? (cheap for research, strong for the review gate)
- [ ] `model: Auto` for mixed work; escalate only when a mid model stalls?
- [ ] Review run **once**, after fixes are pushed (13 premium requests each)?
- [ ] Finish the task, then start a fresh session instead of one ballooning thread?

**To stay out of vibe coding**
- [ ] Acceptance criteria written before code?
- [ ] Tests included, read, and meaningful?
- [ ] Diff reviewed file-by-file, not approved on summary?
- [ ] Security (OWASP) + CVE audit + green CI enforced as hard gates?
- [ ] Humans confirm irreversible actions (repo create, schema change, force-push)?

## 10. Avoiding "vibe coding"

**Vibe coding** is accepting AI output because it *looks* right — no spec, no tests, no
verification. It feels fast and produces unmaintainable, insecure, or subtly broken code.
"Let the AI do as much as possible" and "don't vibe code" are **not** in tension: the
resolution is to make autonomy **bounded by verification, not by trust.**

The model is allowed to do a lot *because* its output must pass gates it cannot talk its
way around:

| Guardrail | Where it lives | What it prevents |
|-----------|----------------|------------------|
| **Specs first** | `epic-planner` / `code-planner` write acceptance criteria before code | Building the wrong thing |
| **TDD + ≥80% coverage** | `code-issue` skill | Untested code paths, regressions |
| **OWASP Top 10 review** | `code-review` skill | Injection, broken auth, secrets, SSRF, etc. |
| **`disallowedTools: Write, Edit` on the reviewer** | `code-review` agent | The reviewer "fixing" instead of reporting; rubber-stamping |
| **CI must be green** | review gate + Orchestrator | Merging broken builds (even pre-existing failures) |
| **Dependency CVE audit** | Orchestrator SECURITY AUDIT phase | Pulling in vulnerable packages |
| **Capped review cycles (max 2)** | Orchestrator | Endless expensive review loops |
| **CHANGELOG discipline** | review + contribution rules | Undocumented user-facing changes |
| **Memory / learnings files** | `/memories/`, repo memory | Re-deriving the same facts every session (also saves tokens) |

## 7. Lever 4 — graphify

> **Superseded for Claude Code agents (2026-07-29).** A measured counterfactual scored
> graphify 2/10 correct at 4× the tokens of native `Grep`/`Glob` on this repo's own
> structural questions, so Claude Code agents navigate with plain search and `Explore`, and
> the graph is kept for humans and CI only. (That measurement pre-dates #1168, which found
> `Grep`/`Glob` are not tools in this build; the search route is now `grep`/`find` via `Bash`,
> which does not change the comparison's outcome.) See
> [docs/decisions/0004-graphify-agent-navigation.md](decisions/0004-graphify-agent-navigation.md).
> The savings figures below are the pre-counterfactual measurement of query output size,
> not of end-to-end answer cost.

### Practical agent rules

- **Restrict `tools:`** to what the agent actually needs. Unused tool schemas are dead
  weight in that agent's window. Example: the review agent does not need write tools.
- **Set `model:` per agent** to the cheapest model that can do the job (see §8).
- **Scope MCP servers to the agent** (`mcpServers:` in Claude Code) so a research agent
  doesn't carry the Playwright browser tool schemas, and a reviewer doesn't carry write
  tools.
- **Use Explore/Plan (Claude Code) or a dedicated research subagent (Copilot)** for
  "where is X / what calls Y" questions — they are the cheapest way to search.
- **Keep the agent body tight.** It is the system prompt; every word is paid each run.

## 11. Worked example

A realistic "add a feature" run, annotated with where tokens go and how each lever helps.

```text
USER: "Add rate limiting to the /api/m365/cleanup endpoint, with tests and a PR."

1. ORCHESTRATOR (balanced model) — delegates; keeps main thread tiny.

2. → research subagent (haiku, mcpServers: context7)
     - looks up express-rate-limit usage via context7 (docs, not source)
     - returns a 150-token summary          ← verbose doc text stayed in the subagent

3. → code-planner subagent (balanced)
     - graphify query "m365 cleanup route"  ← ~2k tokens instead of reading the router tree
     - writes acceptance criteria + 1 sub-issue   ← spec-first, not vibe

4. → code-issue subagent (balanced/inherit)
     - reads ONLY the flagged route file (targeted range, not the whole module)
     - TDD: writes a failing test, implements, runs `vitest run` in the subagent
       (8k tokens of test output stay in the subagent)   ← returns "all green" to main
     - ≥80% coverage enforced               ← gate, not vibe
     - opens PR, updates CHANGELOG [Unreleased]

5. ORCHESTRATOR — SECURITY AUDIT phase
     - `pnpm audit` + OSV.dev lookups for any new dep   ← blocks High/Critical

6. → code-review subagent (strong/inherit, disallowedTools: Write,Edit)
     - OWASP pass (A04 rate limiting is literally the change), CI must be green
     - graphify path <route> <callers> to catch un-updated callers
     - publishes structured review; verdict APPROVE
     - review = 13 premium requests, so it runs ONCE, after fixes are in

7. ORCHESTRATOR — reports: epic/issue #, PR #, coverage, audit result, verdict.
```

Token hot-spots avoided: the express-rate-limit docs, the test output, and the router
exploration were the three largest token sinks — and all three were absorbed by
subagents or replaced by a graphify query, never touching the main window.

## 3. The mental model

Picture the context window as a fixed-size desk. Five things compete for desk space on
every request:

```
┌───────────────────────── context window ─────────────────────────┐
│ system prompt + agent persona                                     │
│ ALWAYS-ON instruction files (copilot-instructions.md / CLAUDE.md) │ ← paid every time
│ tool schemas for every ENABLED tool                               │ ← paid every time
│ invoked skill bodies (persist once loaded)                        │
│ files you read + every tool result + conversation history         │ ← grows during work
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The optimization strategy follows directly:

| If this is large… | …do this |
|---|---|
| Always-on instruction files | Keep them lean; they are paid on every request **and every subagent spawn**. |
| Tool schemas | Enable only the servers/tools you need; rely on tool search to defer the rest. |
| Skill bodies | Keep `SKILL.md` focused; push rarely-needed detail to supporting files read on demand. |
| Files read + tool results | Use graphify to answer structural questions; read targeted line ranges, not whole files; route high-volume output to subagents. |
| Conversation history | Finish a task, then start a fresh session rather than letting one balloon. |

## 2. Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|-----------|
| **Token** | The unit models read/write. ~4 characters / ~0.75 words of English. Pricing and context limits are denominated in tokens. |
| **Context window** | The maximum tokens a model can consider for a single request. Shared across system prompt, instructions, tool schemas, files read, and tool outputs. |
| **Premium request** | Copilot's paid billing unit. 1 per agent/chat prompt × the model's multiplier. Code review = 13. |
| **Model multiplier** | A per-model factor applied to the premium-request cost. Small/fast models are cheaper; frontier models cost more. |
| **Agent** (`.github/agents/*.agent.md` for Copilot | A persona defined by a system prompt + YAML frontmatter (allowed tools, model, sub-agents, handoffs). Frontmatter is loaded when the agent runs. |
| **Subagent** | An agent invoked by another agent (`runSubagent`). Runs in an **isolated context window**; only its final summary returns to the caller. The key tool for keeping verbose work out of the main conversation. |
| **Skill** (`.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) | A reusable, step-by-step workflow. Only its **name + description** sit in context until it is invoked; then the **full body loads** and persists for the rest of the session. |
| **Instruction file** (`.github/instructions/*.instructions.md`) | File-pattern-scoped coding rules. Pulled into context when you touch a matching file (via `applyTo` globs). |
| **Always-on context** (`copilot-instructions.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`) | Project rules auto-loaded into (nearly) every request/subagent. The most expensive lines in the repo because they are paid repeatedly. |
| **MCP server** | A Model Context Protocol server exposing tools (e.g. `github`, `context7`, `tavily`, `playwright`). Defined in `.vscode/mcp.json` / `.mcp.json`. |
| **Tool schema** | The name + description + parameter spec of a tool. Every *enabled* tool's schema occupies context so the model knows the tool exists. |

### Premium requests

GitHub Copilot meters paid usage in **premium requests**. The rules that matter:

- **One user prompt in agent/chat mode = 1 premium request, multiplied by the
  model's multiplier.** A cheaper model has a smaller multiplier; a frontier model
  has a larger one. (See the authoritative, frequently-updated list:
  [GitHub Copilot — auto model selection & multipliers](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/models/auto-model-selection).)
- **Copilot code review costs 13 premium requests per review** (as of 2026-06-01).
  This is why the Orchestrator caps review cycles and only re-reviews after fixes are
  actually pushed — every wasted review cycle is expensive.
- Tool calls the model makes while servicing your prompt do **not** each cost a new
  premium request, but they **do** consume context-window tokens, which is the *other*
  cost you are managing (see below).

> **Two distinct budgets.** (a) *Premium requests* — billed, per-prompt, model-weighted.
> Fewer, better prompts and cheaper models reduce this. (b) *Context-window tokens* —
> the working memory of a single request. Bloated context degrades answer quality and
> can force truncation/compaction. Most techniques in this doc reduce **both**.

### The rule: new objective → new session

> **Start a fresh session when the objective changes. Keep the session when the next
> step serves the same objective.**

| Situation | Do this | Why |
|-----------|---------|-----|
| Finished a feature, starting an unrelated one | **New session** | None of the old context helps; carrying it is pure cost + compaction risk |
| Fixing review comments on the PR you just built | **Same session** | The plan, files, and decisions are load-bearing; re-establishing them would cost more |
| Iterating on the same module / bug | **Same session** | Accumulated context is the working set |
| "OK, totally different thing now…" | **New session** | That phrase is the signal to reset |
| Main thread feels sluggish or is repeating itself | **New session** | Likely already compacting; a reset restores fidelity |

### What an agent costs

When an agent runs, its **system prompt (the whole `.agent.md` body)** and frontmatter
enter context. In Copilot, the Orchestrator pattern runs Plan → Implement → Review in
one session by calling specialized agents as **subagents**.

The critical fact, especially for Claude Code: **a subagent starts with a fresh,
isolated context window.** It does *not* inherit the caller's conversation history. It
*does* reload the always-on project memory (`CLAUDE.md` and the memory hierarchy) plus
a git-status snapshot — **except** the built-in **Explore** and **Plan** subagents,
which skip that memory load. (In Copilot the equivalent saving comes from the subagent
not inheriting the main thread's history.)

> **Consequence.** Chaining six subagents reloads `CLAUDE.md` ~six times. If `CLAUDE.md`
> is 1,650 tokens, that is ~10k tokens spent on memory alone for one orchestrated run.
> **Every line in an always-on file is paid once per delegation.** That is why we keep
> `CLAUDE.md` / `copilot-instructions.md` short and push detail into `docs/` that is
> read only when relevant.

### How an inbound message is ingested

1. **Activity type.** Only `message` activities carry content; everything else is
   ignored.
2. **Bot-own-message guard.** A proactive message #550 sent comes back as an
   activity whose `from.id === recipient.id` (the bot's own id) — ignored before
   any work (see [Loop guard round trip](#loop-guard-round-trip)).
3. **Resolve the link.** `getByConversation(workspaceId, conversationId)` (#549).
   No active link → the channel is not bridged → ignored.
4. **Text.** The leading bot `@mention` markup is stripped (other users'
   mentions preserved); an empty / mention-only message is skipped.
5. **Resolve the sender.** `resolveUserFromAadObjectId(tenantId, aadObjectId)`
   (#549), with `tenantId` taken from the activity's `channelData.tenant.id`,
   then `conversation.tenantId`, then the link's recorded tenant.
6. **Unmapped sender → never attributed to nobody.** When the resolver returns
   `null`, ingestion is **skipped** and a one-time, per-conversation, best-effort
   hint is posted back to the channel inviting the user to link their METIS
   account. No message is created.
7. **Member/tenant authorization.** Identity is not authorization — the resolved
   user is run through `canAccessThread` at the **lowest privilege**
   (`role: "reader"`, so access must be earned through real project membership,
   never a fabricated admin role). A resolved-but-unauthorized sender is rejected
   (forbidden); a link pointing at a missing/soft-deleted thread reports
   not-found.
8. **Create.** `createHumanDiscussionMessage({ ..., origin: "teams" })` — the
   `origin: "teams"` is what makes the #550 outbound mirror skip it.

### The trade-off to be aware of

A reset is not free: each new session reloads the **always-on instruction files**
(`copilot-instructions.md` / `CLAUDE.md`) and re-establishes baseline context. That
fixed re-cost is exactly why (a) those files must stay lean, and (b) you should **not**
reset *mid-task* just for tidiness — you'd pay the reload without shedding any
load-bearing context.

### Progressive disclosure: the whole point of skills

A skill is a workflow document. Copilot/Claude use **progressive disclosure**:

1. **Always in context:** only the skill's **name + `description`** (a few dozen
   tokens). This is how the model knows the skill exists and when to use it.
2. **On invocation:** the **full `SKILL.md` body** loads — and then **stays in context**
   for the rest of the session.

So a 560-line skill costs ~30 tokens until used, then ~8k tokens for the rest of the
session once triggered. Two consequences:

- **Write descriptions that trigger correctly the first time.** A vague description
  causes the wrong skill to fire (wasting a load) or the right one to be missed. Lead
  with the trigger phrase and the "use when / not for" boundaries.
- **Keep `SKILL.md` focused on the common path.** Push rarely-needed reference (large
  lookup tables, exhaustive examples, error-recovery matrices) into supporting files
  that the agent reads *only when it actually needs them*.

> **When to split a skill.** Split only when a large fraction of the body is **rarely
> needed**. If the bulk is the substance the workflow uses on every run (e.g. the OWASP
> table in `code-review`), splitting just adds a read round-trip when the detail is
> needed and saves little — don't fragment a tuned workflow for its own sake. We **did**
> remove duplicated shell-hygiene rules from `code-review/SKILL.md` because that text is
> already in `CLAUDE.md` / `copilot-instructions.md` — dedup is a free win; splitting
> load-bearing content is not.

### Flow on a promote submit

1. **Correlate.** Read `{ threadId, messageId }` from the (untrusted) submit
   `value`. A submit missing either id → graceful error card (`bad-correlation`).
2. **Resolve the acting user.** `resolveUserFromAadObjectId(tenantId, aadObjectId)`
   (#549), tenant-scoped (`channelData.tenant.id`, then `conversation.tenantId`).
   An **unmapped/anonymous** sender → refusal card; **never promote on behalf of
   nobody**.
3. **Authorize.** `canAccessThread` at the **lowest privilege** (`role: "reader"`),
   so access must be earned through real project membership, never a fabricated
   admin role (same posture as #551 inbound). A non-member → refusal card
   (`forbidden`); a missing/soft-deleted thread → `thread-not-found` card.
4. **Verify** the correlated message still exists in the thread (defence in depth
   against a tampered/stale card payload).
5. **Promote** via `promoteMessageToRequirement`, with the **real resolved user**
   as the actor — so the `AuditLog` provenance attributes the promotion to the
   actual Teams user, not the bot. The Requirement title is derived from the
   source message's first non-empty line (clamped to 255, the column limit),
   since the button carries no free-text input.
6. **Respond.** A **confirmation card** (with the new requirement id) on success;
   a **clear refusal/error card** on every failure.

### Why the session itself is a cost

Everything already in the current window — files read, tool results, prior reasoning,
completed todos — **is re-sent with every new prompt you type in that session.** The
conversation is cumulative: a turn 30 prompts deep carries the weight of all 29 before
it. That has three consequences:

1. **You keep paying** (in context-window tokens) for old work on every subsequent turn.
2. When the window fills, the assistant triggers **compaction** — it summarizes/drops
   older content. The summary is lossy and can mangle details you still cared about.
3. **Stale context degrades quality.** The model anchors on earlier files and decisions
   that are no longer relevant, producing worse answers for the new task.

## 9f. Multi-replica uploads store (S3) — `UPLOAD_STORAGE_BACKEND`

Uploaded document blobs (RAG source files) are written to a **local volume**
(`UPLOAD_DIR`, default `data/uploads`), backed in the chart by an **RWO PVC**. An
RWO PVC can be mounted read-write by **at most one node**, so under N>1 replicas
a file the upload request writes on replica A is **invisible** to replica B's
later ingest/read — downloads and re-ingest fail intermittently behind the load
balancer (issue #546, epic #518). This was the last per-pod-locality blocker to
lifting `replicaCount=1`.

Select the shared `s3` backend with `UPLOAD_STORAGE_BACKEND` so any replica reads
what any other replica wrote:

| Environment | `UPLOAD_STORAGE_BACKEND` | Backing store |
|---|---|---|
| local / dev (default) | `local` (or unset) | Local disk under `UPLOAD_DIR`. Per-pod — correct only for a single replica. No new infra. |
| **production / multi-replica** | **`s3`** | **Required for N>1 replicas.** Document blobs are written to an S3 bucket with the same content-hash key layout, so every replica shares one durable, replica-agnostic store. Works against any S3-compatible store (MinIO) via an endpoint override. |

### Why this matters

Every connector credential, BYOK API key, GitHub PAT, webhook secret, and database password stored in METIS is encrypted using AES-256-GCM with a per-secret random salt and IV, derived from `VAULT_MASTER_KEY` via Argon2id (or PBKDF2-SHA512 with 600,000 iterations as a fallback). The key is read from the `VAULT_MASTER_KEY` environment variable at startup; it is **never written to the database, never included in any backup tarball, and never logged**.

The encrypted `Secret.ciphertext` rows travel in the database dump. Without the matching `VAULT_MASTER_KEY` on B, every one of those rows is permanently unrecoverable. There is no escrow, no recovery mechanism, and no support path.

> **If you lose `VAULT_MASTER_KEY`, all secrets stored in METIS are permanently unrecoverable. There is no recovery path.**

In production, when `NODE_ENV=production`, the server **refuses to start** if `VAULT_MASTER_KEY` is absent or decodes to fewer than 32 bytes (`VaultConfigurationError`). See `server/src/lib/vault/vault-service.ts`.

### 4.1 Rotation procedure (operator runbook)

1. **Pre-flight**: take a fresh backup (`./scripts/backup.sh`). If anything goes wrong, you restore from this point.
2. **Generate a new key**:
   ```bash
   NEW_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)
   ```
3. **Stop the application**:
   ```bash
   docker compose stop server ui
   ```
4. **Re-encrypt secrets** under the new key. The vault module supports a version byte on every ciphertext, so historical rows with the old key remain readable while you migrate. Run a one-shot script that:
   - reads every `Vault.entry` row,
   - decrypts using the existing `VAULT_MASTER_KEY`,
   - re-encrypts with `NEW_KEY`,
   - writes back atomically per row (transaction-per-row, so a mid-rotation failure leaves no partial ciphertexts).

   A reference implementation is tracked in follow-up issue #150 (`pnpm vault:rotate` CLI). For v1.0.0, perform rotation by spinning up a one-off container with both keys exported (`VAULT_MASTER_KEY=<old>` + `VAULT_NEXT_KEY=<new>`) and running the rotation Prisma script.
5. **Swap the active key**:
   ```bash
   sed -i 's|^VAULT_MASTER_KEY=.*|VAULT_MASTER_KEY='"$NEW_KEY"'|' .env.prod
   ```
6. **Restart**:
   ```bash
   docker compose --env-file .env.prod -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d
   ```
7. **Verify** `/readyz` reports `vault: ok` and a sample connector still resolves a credential (e.g. trigger a connector refresh from the UI).
8. **Securely destroy the old key** from your secret store / password manager.

## Encrypted vault-key sidecar (`--include-vault-key`)

`pnpm export --include-vault-key` lets the vault master key travel **with** the
export — safely — instead of out-of-band. It encrypts `VAULT_MASTER_KEY` under a
passphrase and writes a **separate** sidecar file next to the tarball:
`<tarball>.vaultkey.enc`.

- **Crypto:** AES-256-GCM with a scrypt-derived key, a per-file random salt, a
  random IV, and a 16-byte auth tag. Self-describing, versioned JSON envelope.
  Source of truth: `server/src/lib/portability/vault-key-cipher.ts`; the `.mjs`
  scripts use the format-compatible sibling `scripts/lib/vault-key-cipher.mjs`.
- **Passphrase handling:** the passphrase is read from the
  `METIS_EXPORT_PASSPHRASE` environment variable **or** an interactive prompt —
  **never from argv** (which would leak into shell history and the process
  table). Weak/empty passphrases are refused (minimum 12 characters).
- **The plaintext key is NEVER written to disk in plaintext and NEVER placed
  inside the tarball.** It exists only inside the passphrase-encrypted sidecar.

### Practices that keep you out of the vibe-coding trap

1. **Write the acceptance criteria before the code.** If you can't state how you'll know
   it works, the model can't either.
2. **Demand tests with the change**, and read them — a test that passes when the
   implementation is wrong is worse than no test.
3. **Read the diff, not the vibe.** Skim every changed file; don't approve on summary
   alone.
4. **Keep the human in the loop at decision points** (repo creation, schema changes,
   force-push, deletes) — these are deliberately not automated.
5. **Make the model cite evidence** (file:line, docs) rather than assert. This is also a
   token *saver* because it discourages the model from re-reading everything to bluff.
6. **Prefer small, verifiable increments** over one giant generated change you can't
   review.

> Autonomy and rigor compound: precise specs and hard gates let you safely hand the model
> *more* work, while also reducing the exploratory token-thrash that comes from vague
> instructions.

### Progressive disclosure: the whole point of skills

A skill is a workflow document. Copilot/Claude use **progressive disclosure**:

1. **Always in context:** only the skill's **name + `description`** (a few dozen
   tokens). This is how the model knows the skill exists and when to use it.
2. **On invocation:** the **full `SKILL.md` body** loads — and then **stays in context**
   for the rest of the session.

So a 560-line skill costs ~30 tokens until used, then ~8k tokens for the rest of the
session once triggered. Two consequences:

- **Write descriptions that trigger correctly the first time.** A vague description
  causes the wrong skill to fire (wasting a load) or the right one to be missed. Lead
  with the trigger phrase and the "use when / not for" boundaries.
- **Keep `SKILL.md` focused on the common path.** Push rarely-needed reference (large
  lookup tables, exhaustive examples, error-recovery matrices) into supporting files
  that the agent reads *only when it actually needs them*.

> **When to split a skill.** Split only when a large fraction of the body is **rarely
> needed**. If the bulk is the substance the workflow uses on every run (e.g. the OWASP
> table in `code-review`), splitting just adds a read round-trip when the detail is
> needed and saves little — don't fragment a tuned workflow for its own sake. We **did**
> remove duplicated shell-hygiene rules from `code-review/SKILL.md` because that text is
> already in `CLAUDE.md` / `copilot-instructions.md` — dedup is a free win; splitting
> load-bearing content is not.

## Provider caveats

The SQLite → SQLite round-trip is exercised on every PR by the CI test `server/src/lib/portability/logical-roundtrip.test.ts` (creates two throwaway SQLite DBs, applies migrations, seeds relational + self-referential + `Secret.ciphertext` + `Json`/`DateTime` data, exports, imports, and asserts byte-identical survival).

The SQLite ↔ **Postgres** variant is **not exercised in CI** — standing up a Postgres server is not available in the default CI sandbox, so there is **no automated cross-provider data test** (it is a [deferred follow-up](#9-deferred-follow-ups)). What CI *does* assert about the Postgres path is its adapter-selection contract: a pure unit test (`server/src/lib/portability/logical-adapter.test.ts`) verifies that selecting `DATABASE_PROVIDER=postgresql` fails loudly with the actionable "install `@prisma/adapter-pg`" message when the adapter is absent, and never silently falls back to the SQLite adapter. Because both schemas are semantically identical (same models/fields; only the datasource provider differs), the same load code path applies once the adapter is installed — but **validate a real cross-provider reload in a staging environment before relying on it in production.**

### 6.1 Embedding-model migration

Changing `EMBED_MODEL` (or `EMBED_POOLING*` / `EMBED_DTYPE`) changes the **vector
space**. Stored vectors are model-tagged, so nothing is corrupted or mis-scored —
but every project's dense retrieval degrades to **BM25-only** until it is
re-embedded, and on `VECTOR_STORE=pgvector` the shared `vector(N)` column must be
migrated before a vector of the new width can be written at all.

```bash
pnpm embeddings:migrate status          # exits non-zero while work remains
pnpm embeddings:migrate prepare --force # pgvector only — destructive to vectors
pnpm embeddings:migrate reindex --all   # per-project shadow build + atomic cutover
```

The reindex is **resumable**: an interrupted run (pod eviction, OOM kill, rolling
deploy) leaves its shadow table as a checkpoint, and re-running the same command
picks up where it stopped. Rollback is a forward operation — chunk text is the
source of truth, so pointing `EMBED_MODEL` back at the old model and reindexing
restores the previous index exactly.

Full runbook, including the EKS specifics, the pgvector column-width path and what
is kept vs lost on a rollback:
[docs/EMBEDDINGS_BACKENDS.md § Runbook](./EMBEDDINGS_BACKENDS.md#runbook--migrating-a-deployment-to-a-new-embedding-model-787).

## 9d. Multi-replica RAG vector store (pgvector) — `VECTOR_STORE`

The RAG dense vector store **defaults to embedded LanceDB**: a per-pod local
directory under `LANCEDB_PATH`. LanceDB is a **single-writer** embedded store —
under N>1 replicas behind the ALB, two pods writing the same data dir (even on an
EFS RWX volume) **corrupt the index** (issue #543, epic #518). Fine for local/dev
(one process); **wrong for any multi-replica deployment.**

Select the shared `pgvector` backend with `VECTOR_STORE` so every replica reads
and writes the same vectors through the shared Postgres:

| Env | Backend | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| local / dev | (unset → embedded LanceDB) | Single process. No external dependency. |
| tests / offline | `local` (or `AI_OFFLINE=1`) | Dependency-free JSON store. |
| **production / multi-replica** | **`pgvector`** | **Required for N>1 replicas.** Reuses the **shared Postgres you already run** (#539's `DATABASE_URL`-scheme-selected adapter) — no extra service. Vectors live in one `rag_vectors` table; Postgres serializes concurrent writers, so the LanceDB corruption mode is gone. |

**Recommended production config (with the shared Postgres from §0):**

```yaml
env:
  DATABASE_URL: postgresql://…   # shared Postgres (required for N>1)
  VECTOR_STORE: pgvector
```

### 7.2 Dockerised MCP Runtime (Epic #271)

The METIS server image no longer bakes in `uvx`, `jbang`, `npx`, etc. Instead,
each MCP server can declare a `runtime` of `docker-stdio`, and the lifecycle
manager spawns a wrapper container per MCP via `docker run -i --rm`. To enable
this on a production host:

1. **Bring up the `metis-mcp` bridge network** (default name `metis-mcp`,
   override with `MCP_DOCKER_NETWORK`). As of Epic #359 the network is
   declared in both `docker-compose.yml` and `docker-compose.prod.yml`, so
   `docker compose up` (or `pnpm bootstrap:up`) **auto-creates it**. Run
   the manual command only when you are running the METIS server outside
   compose:
   ```bash
   # Optional — only needed when METIS itself is not run via docker compose.
   docker network create metis-mcp
   ```
   `pnpm bootstrap:check` (Epic #359 / issue #365) reports the presence of
   this network so you can spot a missing one before the first MCP
   registration. Without the network, every `docker-stdio` MCP fails to
   start with `network metis-mcp not found`.

2. **Mount the Docker socket** into the METIS server container so it can spawn
   sibling containers (already wired in `docker-compose.prod.yml`).

3. **Build & publish the wrapper images** (one-time, repeat on upgrade):
   ```bash
   ./images/mcp-wrappers/build.sh push        # → ghcr.io/metis-mcps/{uvx,jbang,node,npx}-runner:<version>
   ```
   Override the registry with `REGISTRY=… ./images/mcp-wrappers/build.sh push`.

4. **Allow the wrapper images** by adding them to `MCP_IMAGE_ALLOWLIST`
   (Settings → Configuration). The provisioner re-validates the image at
   provision time, so an off-allowlist image is rejected with a structured
   error before any container starts.

### 4.1 Rotation procedure (operator runbook)

1. **Pre-flight**: take a fresh backup (`./scripts/backup.sh`). If anything goes wrong, you restore from this point.
2. **Generate a new key**:
   ```bash
   NEW_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)
   ```
3. **Stop the application**:
   ```bash
   docker compose stop server ui
   ```
4. **Re-encrypt secrets** under the new key. The vault module supports a version byte on every ciphertext, so historical rows with the old key remain readable while you migrate. Run a one-shot script that:
   - reads every `Vault.entry` row,
   - decrypts using the existing `VAULT_MASTER_KEY`,
   - re-encrypts with `NEW_KEY`,
   - writes back atomically per row (transaction-per-row, so a mid-rotation failure leaves no partial ciphertexts).

   A reference implementation is tracked in follow-up issue #150 (`pnpm vault:rotate` CLI). For v1.0.0, perform rotation by spinning up a one-off container with both keys exported (`VAULT_MASTER_KEY=<old>` + `VAULT_NEXT_KEY=<new>`) and running the rotation Prisma script.
5. **Swap the active key**:
   ```bash
   sed -i 's|^VAULT_MASTER_KEY=.*|VAULT_MASTER_KEY='"$NEW_KEY"'|' .env.prod
   ```
6. **Restart**:
   ```bash
   docker compose --env-file .env.prod -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d
   ```
7. **Verify** `/readyz` reports `vault: ok` and a sample connector still resolves a credential (e.g. trigger a connector refresh from the UI).
8. **Securely destroy the old key** from your secret store / password manager.

## 3.4 Full-instance portability (A → B)

To move a complete METIS instance to a fresh host — including the relational database, uploaded documents, and LanceDB vector store — use `pnpm export` (wraps `backup.sh`) on the source instance and `pnpm import` (wraps `restore.sh`) on the target. Both commands support `--dry-run` for safe rehearsal. `VAULT_MASTER_KEY` is never included in any export artifact and must be carried out-of-band via your organisation's secret manager or a sealed channel; without it, all encrypted connector secrets are permanently unrecoverable on the target. For the full ordered procedure, store inventory, fix-up checklist, and cross-provider guidance, see [`docs/DATA_PORTABILITY.md`](./DATA_PORTABILITY.md).

## Azure setup (manual — cannot be scripted from inside METIS)

A developer must perform these steps once in Azure to register the bot:

1. **Create an Azure Bot resource** (Azure Portal → *Create a resource* → *Azure
   Bot*). Choose a **Multi-tenant** (or **Single-tenant**) app type.
2. **Capture the Microsoft App ID** (the bot's app/client id) and **create a
   client secret** (*App registration → Certificates & secrets → New client
   secret*). Copy the secret value immediately — it is shown once.
3. **Set the messaging endpoint** to your public METIS host with the workspace
   routing key, e.g.:
   ```
   https://<your-metis-host>/api/integrations/teams/messages?workspaceId=<workspaceId>
   ```
   (Use the value `GET .../manifest` returns as `messagingEndpoint`.)
4. **Enable the Microsoft Teams channel** on the Azure Bot (*Channels → Microsoft
   Teams*).
5. **Install the credentials in METIS** via
   `POST /api/integrations/teams/workspaces/:workspaceId/install` with the app id,
   the client secret, and (for a single-tenant bot) the tenant id.
6. **Build the Teams app package.** `GET .../manifest` returns a `manifest.json`;
   zip it with a `color.png` (192×192) and `outline.png` (32×32) icon and upload
   the `.zip` to Teams (*Apps → Manage your apps → Upload an app*), or publish it
   to your org's app catalog.
7. **Add the bot to a test channel** and send it a message — METIS captures the
   `ConversationReference` for that conversation. If the channel is **linked** to
   a discussion thread (Phase 1) and your Teams account is **mapped** to a METIS
   user (Phase 1 identity), the message is ingested into that thread (Phase 2
   inbound); an unmapped sender receives a one-time hint to link their account.

### Bot messaging endpoint (called by Teams / Bot Framework)

```
POST /api/integrations/teams/messages?workspaceId=<id>
```

- **Authentication:** the Bot Framework JWT in the `Authorization` header,
  validated by the SDK adapter against the workspace's `MicrosoftAppId`. This
  route is **not** behind METIS user auth (`requireAuth`) — it is authenticated by
  the channel-service JWT, not a METIS session.
- `workspaceId` (query) routes the activity to the right workspace's bot
  credentials. **Missing `workspaceId` → 400.**
- A workspace with **no installed credentials → 403** (`TEAMS_NOT_INSTALLED`). We
  never run an auth-disabled adapter that would accept unsigned activities.
- An **invalid/expired/unsigned** activity → **401** (`TEAMS_ACTIVITY_UNAUTHORIZED`).
- On a valid `message` activity the bot captures/refreshes the
  `ConversationReference` and **ingests the message into the linked discussion
  thread** (Phase 2 inbound, #551 — see
  [Inbound message sync](#inbound-message-sync-phase-2--551)). The Phase 0 echo
  behaviour was removed when inbound ingestion landed.

### How an inbound message is ingested

1. **Activity type.** Only `message` activities carry content; everything else is
   ignored.
2. **Bot-own-message guard.** A proactive message #550 sent comes back as an
   activity whose `from.id === recipient.id` (the bot's own id) — ignored before
   any work (see [Loop guard round trip](#loop-guard-round-trip)).
3. **Resolve the link.** `getByConversation(workspaceId, conversationId)` (#549).
   No active link → the channel is not bridged → ignored.
4. **Text.** The leading bot `@mention` markup is stripped (other users'
   mentions preserved); an empty / mention-only message is skipped.
5. **Resolve the sender.** `resolveUserFromAadObjectId(tenantId, aadObjectId)`
   (#549), with `tenantId` taken from the activity's `channelData.tenant.id`,
   then `conversation.tenantId`, then the link's recorded tenant.
6. **Unmapped sender → never attributed to nobody.** When the resolver returns
   `null`, ingestion is **skipped** and a one-time, per-conversation, best-effort
   hint is posted back to the channel inviting the user to link their METIS
   account. No message is created.
7. **Member/tenant authorization.** Identity is not authorization — the resolved
   user is run through `canAccessThread` at the **lowest privilege**
   (`role: "reader"`, so access must be earned through real project membership,
   never a fabricated admin role). A resolved-but-unauthorized sender is rejected
   (forbidden); a link pointing at a missing/soft-deleted thread reports
   not-found.
8. **Create.** `createHumanDiscussionMessage({ ..., origin: "teams" })` — the
   `origin: "teams"` is what makes the #550 outbound mirror skip it.

# Microsoft Teams app foundation

> Epic #547 (Phase 0, #548). This is the **shared Teams-app foundation** — the bot
> messaging endpoint, per-workspace OAuth install flow, encrypted bot credentials,
> and the `ConversationReference` store. Every other Teams capability layers on
> top of it: the collaboration bridge (#549–#554) and the pre-existing ChatOps
> (#63) and notification-card (#67) epics. **This phase does not yet bridge
> discussions** — it only stands up the plumbing and a health/echo bot.

### Admin install flow (workspace admin only)

All of these require `requireAuth` + `requireWorkspaceRole("admin")` (system
admins bypass workspace RBAC).

```
POST   /api/integrations/teams/workspaces/:workspaceId/install
GET    /api/integrations/teams/workspaces/:workspaceId/installation
DELETE /api/integrations/teams/workspaces/:workspaceId/installation
GET    /api/integrations/teams/workspaces/:workspaceId/manifest?packageId=<guid>&publicHost=https://...&botName=METIS
```

`POST .../install` body:

```jsonc
{
  "appId": "<Azure bot app (client) id — MicrosoftAppId>",
  "appPassword": "<Microsoft App Password / client secret>", // encrypted+vaulted, never stored raw
  "tenantId": "<Azure AD tenant id>",   // required only for a SingleTenant bot
  "appType": "MultiTenant",             // MultiTenant | SingleTenant | UserAssignedMSID
  "label": "Prod bot"                   // optional
}
```

The response (and every read) is **secret-free** — the app password is never
echoed back. Re-installing the same `(workspace, appId)` rotates the stored secret
in place. `DELETE` revokes the installation and soft-deletes the vaulted secret.
